history.text:
September 4th, 476. A teenager named Romulus Augustulus was deposed. No siege. No fire. The crown and scepter were packed up and shipped to Constantinople. Romans went to the market that day like any other.

Because the real end had happened centuries earlier.

In 212, Emperor Caracalla made one decision: he turned "Roman citizen" from a bloodline privilege into a license anyone could get. From that moment, Rome stopped being an empire. It became an identity up for grabs.

And for over twelve hundred years, everyone wanted it.

Here's what makes no sense. The empire died in 476. Except over a thousand years later, people were still lining up to claim they were Roman emperors. Not pretending. Actually filing paperwork. Building legal cases. Going to war over it.

Right now, over 800 million people speak a Roman language as their mother tongue. Spanish. Portuguese. French. Italian. Romanian. All descendants of Latin.

So why would anyone fight over a dead empire's name?

Because it wasn't the empire they wanted. It was the license. And that license was issued in 212—centuries before the empire fell. Caracalla turned Roman citizenship from something you were born into, into something that could be granted. He made identity transferable.

The moment he did that, Rome stopped being a place. It became a claim anyone with the right argument could make.

To understand why that claim is still being made today, you have to go back to the year it all started. 212. The year one emperor changed what it meant to be Roman—and accidentally created a brand that would outlive every empire that tried to kill it.

But here's the thing about that moment in 476. It wasn't actually the beginning of the end. The real end had already happened 264 years earlier. In 212 AD, a Roman emperor made a decision that would turn this identity into something nobody could kill—not even when the empire itself collapsed.

His name was Caracalla. And what he did was simple: he looked at the empire and saw a problem nobody was talking about.

First: what did Roman citizenship actually mean before 212?

It wasn't something you could just become. It was inherited. It belonged to people born in Rome proper, to soldiers who'd earned it through military service, to a small administrative class. Everyone else—maybe 90 percent of the empire's population—lived under provincial law. They had no citizenship. No legal protection as Romans. No voting rights, no property inheritance guarantees, no claim to the empire's legal system.

Roman citizenship was the most valuable thing you could own. It meant access to courts that protected your property. It meant your children inherited what you left them. Centuries of emperors had treated it like a crown they could give to generals as a reward for loyalty. It was scarce. It was powerful. It was everything.

So what did Caracalla see that changed his mind?

By 212, the empire was starting to crack. The Severan dynasty—a non-Italian family from Africa and Syria—had seized power in 193. They looked at the map and saw what earlier emperors had missed. The empire's tax base was shrinking because most people paying taxes weren't citizens. Local loyalty was fragmenting because people had no stake in calling themselves Roman. The center was losing gravity.

So in 212, Caracalla did something almost nobody expected. He issued the Constitutio Antoniniana. Almost every free person in the empire, whether they were born in Rome or born thousands of miles away, could now have Roman citizenship.

Not through conquest. Not through marriage. Not through serving in the army for 25 years. Just by decree.

Suddenly, citizenship stopped being a birthright and became something transferable. Something grantable. Something that could be given, inherited, claimed.

Why did he do it? Three reasons, and they all mattered. First was practical: more citizens meant more tax revenue. Only Roman citizens paid certain taxes, especially the inheritance tax. Expanding the citizen class meant expanding the tax base.

Second was religious. The Severan dynasty brought ideas from the non-Latin world—from Syria, from Africa—and they believed in a more universal vision of Roman identity. Not "Roman" as a bloodline, but "Roman" as a philosophy that could spread.

Third was political ideology. Caracalla's advisors—men like the jurist Ulpian—had argued that citizenship shouldn't be a privilege for a lucky minority. That the future of empires belonged to whoever could convince the most people that they belonged.

So when Caracalla signed that edict, he wasn't just expanding citizenship numbers. He was changing the game. He was taking something defined by birth and turning it into something that could be deliberately granted by someone in power. He was making identity portable.

And here's what he probably didn't realize: he had just created something that would outlast him. Would outlast the empire. Would become more valuable after Rome stopped existing than it ever was while Rome ruled everything.

Because now, whenever the empire weakened, whenever a new power rose somewhere else, whenever someone wanted to claim legitimacy, they could point back to this moment in 212 and say: "Caracalla proved that you don't have to be born Roman to be Roman. You just have to be granted it. You just have to claim it with the right argument."

He gave the world a template. And 264 years later, when the empire itself died, that template would become the most contested piece of real estate in the medieval world.

264 years later, on September 4th, 476, that template got its first real test.

Odoacer didn't kill the boy emperor. He didn't declare himself emperor. He just told Romulus Augustulus to step down, gave him a pension, and sent him to live with relatives. That was it. The Western Roman Empire ended with a retirement package.

Then Odoacer took the imperial regalia and shipped them east to Constantinople. The message was clear: "The West doesn't need its own emperor anymore. You're the only one now."

Compare that to 410. When the Visigoth king Alaric sacked Rome, Saint Jerome said: "The city which had taken the whole world was itself taken." It felt like the end of the world. But by 476, Romans had been watching the empire crumble for two generations. The death barely registered.

And yet, something didn't die.

The Roman Senate kept meeting. After 476, with no Western emperor to answer to, the Senate continued to pass decrees and maintain Roman civic life. The last recorded Senate activity was in 603—127 years after the "fall." In 630, the Senate House was converted into a church. That's over 150 years later.

This is the paradox: the political entity died, but the institutional infrastructure kept running. The legal system didn't vanish overnight. The aqueducts didn't stop flowing. Latin didn't stop being the language of administration. And most importantly, the identity didn't expire.

Odoacer's decision to ship the crown east instead of destroying it or wearing it himself—that was the signal. It meant the title of Roman Emperor was no longer bound to one man in one city. It was transferable. It was a license that could be reassigned. Caracalla had made "Roman citizen" a status anyone could receive. Now, in 476, "Roman Emperor" became a title anyone could claim—if they had the right argument.

For the next 324 years, there was only one holder: the Eastern Roman Empire in Constantinople. They were the uncontested keepers of the license. But in the year 800, someone in the West decided they wanted it back.

And the question wasn't whether they had the right bloodline, or whether they controlled Rome itself. The question was: what argument would they use to prove they were the real heir?

Now, tracking all of this—1,241 years of identity claims, five different legitimacy arguments, empires rising and falling across three continents—gets complicated fast.

Which is where today's sponsor comes in: Timeline Studio, a visual research tool built for exactly this kind of problem. It lets you map out complex historical events, connect them with cause-and-effect links, and see patterns you'd miss in a linear document.

For something like Roman succession, you can plot every claimant from 212 to 1453 on one screen: Caracalla's decree here, the 476 collapse there, Charlemagne's coronation, Mehmed II's claim, all linked by the threads of legitimacy each one used. You can tag by argument type—religious authorization, capital occupation, institutional inheritance—and instantly see which strategies lasted longest.

If you're researching any historical topic with overlapping timelines and competing narratives, it's worth checking out. Link in the description.

But back to 800. Because the man who broke Constantinople's 324-year monopoly didn't just want the title. He wanted the entire world to watch him take it.

Christmas Day, 800. Rome. A Frankish king walked into St. Peter's Basilica. He walked out as something that hadn't existed in the West for 324 years: a Roman Emperor.

His name was Charlemagne. When Pope Leo III placed that crown on his head, the identity stopped being a monopoly. The Pope was saying: "Rome isn't dead. It just moved."

Here's what made this work. Method One: Religious Authorization. The Pope's blessing became the legitimacy engine. If the Pope crowns you, you're the continuation of Roman imperial authority. This argument got copied for the next thousand years.

But Charlemagne's method wasn't the only one. 653 years later, someone used a completely different argument—and it worked just as well.

May 29, 1453. Constantinople falls. The 21-year-old Ottoman Sultan Mehmed II walks through the shattered gates. And then he does something unexpected: he claims the identity.

Mehmed gave himself the title Qayser-i Rûm—Caesar of Rome. His logic? Method Two: Capital Occupation. Whoever controls the imperial capital is the Roman Emperor. Constantinople had been the seat of Roman power for 1,123 years. By Mehmed's reasoning, he wasn't conquering Rome—he was becoming Rome.

The Eastern Orthodox Church recognized his title. The West did not. Legitimacy wasn't universal. It was up for negotiation.

Two claimants. Two different justifications. But there's a third method, and this one doesn't even require calling yourself an emperor.

1776 to 1787. Philadelphia. Method Three: Institutional Inheritance. The upper legislative chamber? Senate. The building where Congress meets? The Capitol. The republic itself? Res publica. The U.S. House of Representatives has fasces—the Roman symbol of authority—carved into the walls. The Founding Fathers didn't need a Pope or a conquered city. They inherited Rome by replicating its system.

Method Four: Geographic Symbolism. Around 1510, a Russian monk named Philotheus wrote: "Two Romes have fallen. The third stands. And a fourth there will not be." Moscow claimed to be the Third Rome—the successor to Rome and Constantinople. The logic? Rome fell in 476. Constantinople fell in 1453. Moscow, as the last free Orthodox Christian power, was the rightful heir.

Method Five: International Recognition. 1606: the Peace of Zsitvatorok. The Ottoman Sultan formally recognizes the Holy Roman Emperor as "Caesar." It's symbolic, carefully worded "as father to son," but it's recognition. The title could be shared, transferred, diplomatically endorsed.

In 1472, the niece of the last Byzantine Emperor married Ivan III of Moscow. A wedding became a legitimacy transfer.

Five methods. Religious authorization. Capital occupation. Institutional inheritance. Geographic symbolism. International recognition. None required rebuilding the Roman Empire. They only required one thing: a convincing story about why you were Rome now.

Between 800 and 1453, at least five different political entities found a way that worked for them.

But how long did these claims last? And what did all these claimants have in common?

Start with the timeline. From 212, when Caracalla turned citizenship into a license, to 1453, when the last Byzantine emperor fell, that's 1,241 years. Not a gap. A relay race.

And here's the thing about institutions outlasting the empires that spawned them. The Western Roman Empire collapsed in 476. The Senate? Kept meeting. Last recorded session: 603. That's 127 years after the empire "ended." The Senate chamber wasn't converted into a church until 630—over 150 years post-collapse.

Compare that to the Holy Roman Empire. Started in 962. Dissolved by Napoleon in 1806. 844 years. Longer than the original Roman Empire in the West ever lasted. Hundreds of emperors, all claiming they were the legitimate successors to Rome, all investing resources to keep that claim alive. This wasn't one guy's vanity project. This was a succession of regimes betting their legitimacy on a brand that had been "defunct" for centuries.

The investment wasn't just time. It was geography. Charlemagne's empire covered modern France, Germany, northern Italy. The Holy Roman Empire stretched across Central Europe. Mehmed's Ottoman claim extended from the Balkans through Anatolia to the Levant. Moscow's Third Rome theory positioned Russia as the guardian of Orthodox Christianity. And then the Americans—across the Atlantic, two thousand years away from the original Rome—copied the Senate, the Capitol, the fasces symbols.

The geographic spread tells you this wasn't about proximity to Rome the city. It was about proximity to Rome the idea.

Now the numbers we opened with. 1,241 years from Caracalla's edict to Mehmed's conquest. At least six major claimants across that span: the Byzantines, the Carolingians, the Holy Roman emperors, the Ottomans, the Russians, the Americans. Three continents. And the 800 million to 900 million native speakers of Romance languages as of 2026? That's the linguistic descendant pool of people whose ancestors got Roman citizenship after 212. The legal systems in continental Europe and Latin America? Built on Justinian's Corpus Juris Civilis from 529. The U.S. Capitol still has fasces carved into the walls.

The identity didn't die in 476. It fragmented, multiplied, and spread.

But here's the strange part. All these claimants—emperor after emperor, sultan, tsar, founding father—almost never tried to rebuild the Roman Empire itself. They didn't reconquer all the old provinces. They didn't restore the Senate as a functioning body. Most didn't even speak Latin.

So what were they actually fighting over?

They were fighting over the name itself. The symbol. Not the power—the branding.

Think about it this way. In 212, Caracalla made one decision: he turned "Roman citizen" from a bloodline privilege into something anyone could get. That one move created an infinite loop. Once you turn an exclusive title into a transferable license, it never dies. It just keeps getting inherited.

Which is why an empire that ended in 476 still has applicants lined up in 2026. Charlemagne didn't want to rule Rome—he wanted to be Rome. Mehmed II didn't occupy Constantinople to restore Latin; he occupied it to claim the title "Qayser-i Rûm." The American founders didn't replicate Roman law because they needed it; they named their Senate and Capitol and carved fasces into marble because they wanted to inherit the brand.

Rome stopped being an empire. It became a permission slip.

And here's the contrast. In 212, being Roman was a privilege maybe a million people could access. Today, 800 to 900 million people speak Romance languages as their mother tongue—descended from Latin. A billion more live under legal systems built on Justinian's code. They gather in buildings with Corinthian columns and debate in chambers decorated with Roman symbols.

That's not coincidence. That's the design. That's what happens when you stop gatekeeping identity and start licensing it.

But everyone who lined up to claim this identity knew one thing: you'd get mocked for it.

In 1756, the philosopher Voltaire published his Essay on Customs and delivered what became the most famous insult to this whole imperial claim. He wrote that the Holy Roman Empire was "in no way holy, in no way Roman, and in no way an empire." It was a perfect three-part takedown. And he was right—by every literal measure, the name didn't fit the thing.

Yet the rulers of the Holy Roman Empire read that insult, shrugged, and kept the title anyway. They held it for 844 years after Charlemagne's coronation. They endured the mockery. They signed documents with "Roman Emperor" on them even when everyone knew it meant almost nothing.

Here's where it gets stranger: the official Latin name for this entity—Sacrum Romanum Imperium—didn't appear in formal documentation until 1254. That's 454 years after Charlemagne got crowned. For four and a half centuries, people were already fighting over this identity, already building institutions around it, already making alliances based on it. But the official name? Still not written down.

People weren't fighting over the name itself. They were fighting over something the name represented—a claim, a connection, a status that mattered independent of whether anyone had bothered to write it down correctly.

Then there's the matter of who got to claim it. When Charlemagne got crowned in the West, the Byzantine emperor in Constantinople said it was illegitimate. When Mehmed II conquered Constantinople in 1453 and declared himself Qayser-i Rûm, the Eastern Orthodox church accepted his claim—but Western Christendom rejected it entirely. Same title. Same logic: I control the capital, I inherit the empire. But the Eastern church said yes and the Western church said absolutely not.

It wasn't until 1606, in a peace treaty between the Ottomans and the Holy Roman Emperor, that the Sultan formally acknowledged the Western emperor as "Caesar"—but the phrasing was "as a father to a son," preserving Ottoman precedence.

So here's what everyone debated: Which version was real? Whose right to call themselves Roman actually stood?

The answer, for 1,200 years, was: all of them. And none of them.

They kept claiming it anyway. Why would you endure Voltaire's mockery, navigate the contradiction of ruling an empire that everyone knows isn't Roman, and risk having your claim rejected by half of Christendom?

Because the name was worth more than the mockery. The identity was worth more than the empire.

Here's the thing about the person who made all this possible: Caracalla never saw what he created.

In 217 AD, just five years after he signed that edict, he was stabbed to death by his own guard. He was 29.

But that decision he made in 212? It didn't die with him. It kept going.

We're now in 2026. That's 1,814 years later. Walk into the U.S. Capitol building right now, and you'll see Roman columns. The Senate chamber. The Capitol. The fasces carved into the walls. The founding fathers didn't just copy Rome's politics. They copied its DNA into the architecture, into the words, into the system itself.

Because that's how it works: institutions outlive people. Caracalla's been dead for 1,800 years. But the thing he turned into a permission slip—Roman identity—got inherited by every system that wanted legitimacy after him.

So the real question isn't "Was Charlemagne really Roman?" or "Was Mehmed II really Roman?" The real question is: what makes an identity so durable that it survives empires, religions, centuries of mockery—and still matters?

This story teaches us two things.

First: when you turn an identity from an exclusive privilege into something anyone can get, you create a permission slip that never expires. 212 to 1453 is 1,241 years—that's how long the application line stayed open. But it didn't stop there. Eight to nine hundred million people speak Romance languages today. Modern legal systems across Europe and Latin America run on Roman law. The U.S. Capitol, the Senate, the fasces decorating the walls—all Roman design language. All of this is downstream from that 212 decision.

Caracalla turned citizenship into a license. That license became inheritable. And now it's so widespread most people don't even know they're using it.

Second: institutions and symbols outlive the empires that build them. The Roman Empire died in 476. But "Rome" as a name, as a concept, as a brand—it's still here. That name carried something more valuable than land or armies. It carried a whole system—legal frameworks, political philosophy, architectural language, legitimacy itself.

That's why it wasn't "false advertising" when the Holy Roman Empire got mocked. The mockery proved the point: they weren't claiming land, they were claiming identity. The name itself didn't belong to the empire. It belonged to a symbol system that could be redefined forever.

Don't sell the empire. Sell the identity.

Maybe only one identity lasted longer.

Christianity? Islam? American democracy? Each claimed to be universal, each survived the collapse of empires. Next time, we'll see which one learned from Rome—and which one tried to replace it.

Until then.

Before 212, Roman citizenship was unavailable to most people in the empire. It could come through birth or be granted for service and other reasons. Most people lived under local legal systems, rather than the protections and privileges attached to Roman citizenship.

Caracalla belonged to the Severan dynasty, which had seized power in 193. Why did he do it? One explanation is practical: extending citizenship could bring more people within reach of taxes that applied to Roman citizens, including the inheritance tax.

But Charlemagne's method wasn't the only one. 653 years later, someone used a completely different argument—and it worked just as well.

On May 29, 1453, the Ottoman sultan Mehmed II captured Constantinople, ending the Eastern Roman Empire. He then claimed the title Qayser-i Rûm, or Caesar of Rome.

Mehmed's claim rested on control of the former imperial capital. Constantinople had served as the Eastern Roman capital since 330, a span of 1,123 years by the time it fell. His argument was that control of the city gave him a claim to Roman imperial succession.

Mehmed appointed the Orthodox patriarch, continuing an important imperial practice. That does not by itself establish formal church recognition of his Qayser-i Rûm title; western Christian authorities generally rejected his claim.

These claims rested on different grounds. A later example shows how Roman political influence could travel without anyone claiming to be a Roman emperor.

The American founders drew on Roman republican language and symbols, but that was not a claim to be the Roman Empire. The Senate first met in 1789 at Federal Hall in New York; construction of the Capitol began in 1793, and the Senate first met there in 1800. The House chamber still displays fasces, a Roman symbol of authority.

In the early sixteenth century, the monk Philotheus advanced the idea of Moscow as the Third Rome: after Rome and Constantinople, Moscow would be the center of Orthodox Christianity. The dating of his letters is debated, so the claim is best placed broadly in that period.

In 1606, the Peace of Zsitvatorok marked a shift in Ottoman usage: Sultan Ahmed I recognized Rudolf II as a caesar rather than merely as a king. The wording preserved Ottoman precedence; it was a diplomatic acknowledgment, not a transfer of imperial authority.

In 1472, a niece of the last Byzantine emperor married Ivan III of Moscow. Later accounts connected the marriage to Moscow's claims of Byzantine succession, but the marriage itself was not a formal transfer of legitimacy.

Across these cases, rulers and writers invoked different grounds: papal coronation, control of Constantinople, or the legacy of Roman republican institutions. These were distinct claims, and they were not accepted by everyone.

From the eighth century onward, multiple political powers made claims to Roman imperial legitimacy, though their grounds and recognition differed.

But how long did these claims last? And what did all these claimants have in common?

Caracalla's decree came in 212; Constantinople fell in 1453. That is 1,241 years, but it is not a 1,241-year chain of imperial succession claims.

The Holy Roman Empire lasted from 962 until 1806, a span of 844 years. Its rulers claimed a connection to Roman imperial authority across many generations, though the empire was not simply the same state continued from Charlemagne's coronation.

The investment wasn't just time. It was geography. Charlemagne's empire covered modern France, Germany, northern Italy. The Holy Roman Empire stretched across Central Europe. Mehmed's Ottoman claim extended from the Balkans through Anatolia to the Levant. Moscow's Third Rome theory positioned Russia as the guardian of Orthodox Christianity. And then the Americans—across the Atlantic, two thousand years away from the original Rome—copied the Senate, the Capitol, the fasces symbols.

These examples show that claims to Rome could rest on more than control of the city itself. They do not all amount to the same kind of political succession.

The span from 212 to Mehmed II's conquest in 1453 is 1,241 years. Across the centuries, Byzantines, western emperors, Ottomans, and Russian rulers made different claims to Roman succession. Separately, Roman cultural legacies continued through Romance languages, legal traditions influenced by Roman law, and Roman symbols in American public buildings. Those legacies are not evidence that their speakers or users claim to be Roman emperors.

The Western Empire ended in 476. Claims to Roman imperial legitimacy later multiplied, while Roman cultural and legal legacies followed their own paths.

These cases are not interchangeable. Some rulers claimed Roman imperial succession; the American founders instead drew on Roman republican language and symbols, without claiming to be the Roman Empire.

So what were they actually fighting over?

[CH07 | 13:42-14:54 | 元评论段，揭示所有申领者的共同策略本质，完成主体重定义，用起点与现状的倒置对照震撼观众]

The cases do not add up to a single law of succession. Charlemagne's claim rested on papal coronation. Mehmed II's rested on holding Constantinople. The American founders used Roman republican forms without claiming an empire. Each claim answered a different political need, and none of them turned Caracalla's citizenship decree into a rule for choosing an emperor.

Recognition mattered, too. Michael I formally recognized Charlemagne's imperial title in 812, while western Christian authorities generally rejected Mehmed's claim. The contrast shows that a claim's force depended in part on who accepted it. Together, these cases show that Rome's legacy remained available for political use, but they do not make Caracalla's 212 citizenship decree a license to inherit the throne.

Claims to Rome did not go unchallenged. Some were mocked; others were rejected by rival powers.

In his 1756 Essay on Customs, Voltaire famously mocked the Holy Roman Empire as neither holy, Roman, nor an empire. His line captured a later criticism of the institution's name; it was a polemic, not a neutral description of every aspect of its history.

The Holy Roman Empire lasted from 962 to 1806, or 844 years. That span begins with Otto I's imperial coronation, not Charlemagne's in 800. Voltaire's later satire questioned the name, but it does not tell us how individual rulers reacted to it.

The full Latin name Sacrum Romanum Imperium appears in formal documents by 1254, 454 years after Charlemagne's coronation. That gap shows that the political tradition and its later formal name did not emerge at the same moment; it does not prove that rulers were fighting over one unchanged identity throughout.

The delayed formal name is evidence that Roman political language developed over time. It cannot, by itself, show what every ruler believed the name represented.

In 800, Empress Irene ruled in Constantinople. She sought a settlement with Charlemagne, but faced opposition in the East; her successor Michael I formally recognized Charlemagne's imperial title in 812. Centuries later, Mehmed II claimed Qayser-i Rûm after taking Constantinople. He appointed the Orthodox patriarch, but that does not establish formal church recognition of his title; western Christian authorities generally rejected his claim.

In 1606, the Peace of Zsitvatorok marked a shift in Ottoman usage by recognizing Rudolf II as a caesar rather than merely as a king. The diplomatic wording preserved Ottoman precedence.

No single power settled these claims. Some rulers recognized a title that rivals rejected; others borrowed Roman institutions without claiming to be emperor. Voltaire could mock the Holy Roman Empire's name, and the formal Latin title could arrive centuries late, yet the political language still carried weight. That did not mean all claimants sought the same thing.

Caracalla did not live to see the later history of Roman citizenship. He was killed in 217, five years after issuing the decree, at the age of 29.

From 212 to 2026 is 1,814 years. Roman influence remains visible in language, law, and American civic symbols, but those inheritances do not show that the United States claimed to be the Roman Empire.

Institutions and symbols can outlast the people who created or used them. But later rulers' claims to Roman legitimacy drew on their own political arguments, not on a succession rule established by Caracalla.

Caracalla's decree and later claims to Roman imperial legitimacy belong to different parts of this story. Together, they raise a narrower question: why did so many later powers find Rome's political legacy useful?

Start with the distinction the evidence supports: Caracalla expanded citizenship, but he did not set up a rule for imperial succession. The 1,241 years from 212 to 1453 connect two events; they do not show a continuous line of applicants. Romance languages, Roman law, and American civic symbols are later inheritances with their own histories.

Caracalla widened access to Roman citizenship. Later claims to Roman imperial legitimacy arose through separate political arguments.

Second, institutions and symbols can outlast the political entities associated with them. The Western Empire ended in 476, while the Eastern Roman Empire continued until 1453. Roman law, political language, and symbols later influenced other societies, but influence is not the same as imperial succession.

The Holy Roman Empire's contested name shows that claims to Rome could be criticized as well as used for legitimacy. That does not prove the name belonged to a timeless system, or that the empire's rulers were not also pursuing political power.

An empire can end while arguments over its legacy continue.
